lines: A team bolts twelve new quality checks onto their orders pipeline, one busy week.

Overnight, the whole thing's runtime doubles. And two weeks later, a bad partition still reaches the dashboard anyway — the one check that would've actually caught it ran only after the data was already published.
So, three checks: one for a missing value, one for freshness, one for drift.
Before the data's published, or after? And here's the real question underneath that one — which of those two choices actually doubled the cost in the first place? Think it through before I go on.
answer: It's not running checks early that costs you. A check sitting before publish only touches data already moving through — that's genuinely cheap.
What actually doubled the cost is a full scan after the fact, reading the entire table back again from scratch, on top of everything the pipeline was already doing.

lines: So, where should a check actually sit?
One option sits before publish and can stop bad data cold — and because it's only touching what's already passing through, it stays cheap.
The other runs after the data's already landed. It can't block anything at that point — and it costs a full read of whatever it's covering.
Now, one particular tool draws a line between two genuinely different kinds of test.
One kind queries data that's already been built, hunting for rows that break an assertion — and on an actual run just now, it caught a real missing customer id.
The other kind checks a model's own logic against fixed, made-up rows, before anything gets built at all — and that one passed clean.
A different tool groups several of these assertions together and runs them all against one batch of data at once.

On the exact same rows, it caught that same missing id all over again — and it caught one more thing entirely: a negative amount, something none of the first tool's four built-in checks had ever been watching for.
A few more tools, worth naming, even though none of them actually ran here.

One checks data against a published contract. Another's built on a distributed engine, turning checks into jobs that compute a metric first, then test the metric itself. A third is built specifically for one platform's own pipelines.
None of their machinery exists on this particular build — so they're named, sourced, and nothing more.
Here's a cheaper way to keep a running check up to date.
Compute a metric on whatever's new, then merge it into what's already stored — instead of rescanning the entire history every single time.
Run it both ways on the same data, and they land on the exact same number. The merged version just gets there for a fraction of the work.
Cheaper still: read a slice instead of everything, and estimate from there.

On this very data, a one-in-ten slice landed on the same relative row every single time it ran — and it missed a bad row that was genuinely there, reporting back zero when the real count wasn't zero at all.
Not a smaller number than the truth. A flat miss.
So, pulling this all together.

A check before publish stays cheap and can block; one after can't block, and costs a full read. One kind of test checks what got built; the other checks the logic behind it. A group of assertions runs together, against one batch.
Compute a metric incrementally, and it matches a full rescan exactly, for far less work. Sample instead, and it's cheaper again — but now it can miss something completely.
One more scenario, and it's worth sitting with.
Picture a check that sits before publish — so it is, by definition, a gate — but it scans every single row of a table that just keeps growing, on every single run, start to finish.
As that table keeps growing, does this gate's own cost per run stay flat, or does it keep climbing? And why?
answer: Climbing. Sitting before publish only tells you when a check runs and whether it can block — it tells you nothing at all about what that check actually costs to compute.
This particular gate rereads the whole table from scratch, every single run — so its cost tracks the table's own size, growing right alongside it, gate or no gate.
